name: Metabolism
summary: A Japanese style of fixed concrete cores that carry replaceable capsules. Its architects drew the city as a living body that grows, changes and renews its cells.

philosophy.core_thesis: A city lives like an organism, so its long-life cores must stand fixed and its short-life cells must change.
design_principles: Separate the fixed structure from the units that people replace.
Plan for growth: leave the frame open at the end and on top.
Hang prefabricated capsules on a core of services and stairs.
Show the core as a monumental concrete tower and the capsules as small machines.
Treat the unit as a product that a factory makes and a crane lifts.
Lift the city above the ground, the sea or old streets on huge platforms.
anti_patterns: A closed, finished building that cannot grow
Capsules that look like part of the wall and hide their joints
Fixed room layouts that tie the user to one plan
Low, spread-out forms with no central core
Rough, hand-built finishes on the capsule

massing.form: A tall concrete core or a pair of cores with many small boxes fixed to its sides; the boxes stack at different heights.
massing.proportion: Vertical towers dominate, and the small cells make a rough, jagged edge on the main shape.
massing.roof: Flat roofs; the core ends in a plain parapet or a plant room.
massing.relation_to_ground: The core stands on a raised base, on pilotis or over water, so that the cells float above the street.

structure.system: A reinforced concrete core or megastructure frame with steel or precast cells that bolt to it.
structure.span_and_module: A cell of about 2.5 by 4m is the module, and the cores sit about 10 to 20m apart.
structure.expression: Cores, bolts, ducts and crane hooks stay visible, and the joints between core and cell are the main detail.

materials.finish: The core keeps a bare concrete finish, and the capsules have a smooth, factory-made metal skin with a round window.

palette.name: Signal red
palette.role: small accents on doors and lifts

facade.composition: Plain cores with clusters of identical capsules, each with one round or square window.
facade.openings: One circular porthole window of about 1.3m in each cell.
facade.solid_to_void: Solid dominates: windows cover 10–25% of the elevation.

light_and_space.daylight: Each cell gets light from one window, and the core has narrow slots and stair windows.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: The route runs through the core by lift and stair, and then the visitor enters a small cell with a fixed plan.
light_and_space.interior_character: The cell is a tight, built-in room of about 10 square metres, with a bed, a desk and a bath moulded in one unit.

ornament.attitude: No applied ornament; the repeated capsule and the exposed bolt form the pattern.

rules.rule: Give the fixed core the first place and the cells the second.
Repeat the same cell around the core with small shifts.
Cluster the cells in groups on the core, not in a flat row.
Set the smooth capsule against the raw concrete.
Run all routes through the core and lift.

images.title: Capsules of the Nakagin Capsule Tower

emotion.target_response: Wonder at a city that changes: the viewer feels a machine for the future that has cells like a body.

avoid_when: The brief asks for a low, warm, hand-built domestic place.
The scene needs a flat grid with no central tower.

modifiers.how: Make the cells from board-marked concrete, deepen the windows and remove the smooth metal skin.

sources.title: Kisho Kurokawa, Metabolism in Architecture (Studio Vista, 1977)
